I am a 47-year-old farmer with six years of schooling. I manage eight mu of flat, irrigated land in Quzhou County, the same plot my family has farmed for generations. I do not experiment much—what works in our village is what I do.

This year, like every year, I will grow winter wheat followed by summer maize on all eight mu. That is the rotation our land and climate are built for. The wheat goes in around National Day in autumn, sleeps through winter, and fills grain in May and June. As soon as the wheat comes off in early June, I plant maize directly into the stubble without ploughing. By early October the maize is dry and ready, and I sow wheat again. Two crops, one mu, every year. I have thought about cotton because some neighbours talk about better prices, but cotton needs more labour and the price jumps around. Wheat and maize have stable demand and I know exactly how to grow them.

For wheat, I will use Luyuan 502—an improved variety that the seed shop in town has stocked for years. It is not a hybrid, but it is much better than the old seeds my grandfather used. I will rotary-till the ground before sowing and put down about 30 jin of seed per mu. For fertilizer, I trust compound fertilizer at planting—about 100 jin per mu—and then I topdress with urea at green-up and jointing. All together that works out to roughly 50 kg of nitrogen per mu, plus some phosphate and potash from the compound bag. I irrigate three times: once at green-up after winter, once at jointing, and once at grain filling. My well and the village pump make that possible. I spray pesticides four times: herbicide once early, insecticide twice when aphids and armyworms show up, and fungicide once if I see rust. I expect about 500 kg per mu if the spring weather holds.

For maize, I buy Denghai 605 hybrid seed. It is expensive—around 60 yuan per mu—but the yield is worth it. I plant about one bag per mu, no-till, straight into the wheat stubble. Maize needs less nitrogen than wheat because the soil is still warm and the stubble breaks down; I give it compound fertilizer at sowing and one side-dressing of urea at the big-flare stage, totaling about 22 kg nitrogen per mu. I irrigate twice: once right after sowing if it is dry, and once at the tasseling-silking stage. Three pesticide sprays are enough—herbicide at the start, insecticide twice for corn borers. I expect about 550 kg per mu.

I keep things simple. I follow the calendar, watch what my neighbours do, and buy inputs from the same shop I have used for ten years. That is how I farm.
